fatal_errors: The proposed material is untreated Q235 carbon steel, whereas the target concerns an AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy coating deposited on SS316L.
The central intervention—atmospheric plasma spraying followed by 2 h annealing, particularly at 550 °C—is entirely absent.
The proposed NaCl immersion at 25–150 °C does not reproduce the target environments of 3.5 wt% H2SO4 electrochemistry or cyclic molten-salt corrosion at 900 °C.

The cited evidence does not support the claimed temperature-dependent oxide-film breakdown mechanism in untreated Q235 steel. E1 only documents an electrochemical protocol, while E2 investigates a different HEA coating on Q235.
Aqueous testing at 150 °C requires a pressurized autoclave and high-temperature-compatible reference-electrode methodology, neither of which is specified.
explanation: The hypothesis is internally testable at a generic level, and its use of temperature series, polarization, EIS, and post-exposure microscopy could distinguish an acceleration of chloride corrosion. However, it does not reconstruct the target material system, treatment, conditions, structural mediator, or comparative outcomes. The target mechanism depends on an APS AlCoCrFeNi layer, annealing-induced grain refinement and phase balance, and formation of Al- and Cr-rich protective products; the generated mechanism instead invokes generic chloride penetration of an oxide film on bare Q235. Its baseline also lacks the required uncoated SS316L, as-sprayed coating, and annealed coating comparisons. The falsification rule is directionally useful but vague about effect size and does not isolate oxide-film breakdown from ordinary Arrhenius acceleration, oxygen-solubility changes, or altered solution chemistry. Because the supplied citations establish neither the asserted untreated-Q235 mechanism nor its elevated-temperature behavior, this is not a well-supported alternative despite being experimentally approachable.
